title: HTTP Authentication: Basic and Digest Access Authentication
summary: Specifies HTTP's authentication framework and two schemes, Basic, which sends a username and password, and Digest, which uses cryptographic hashes so the password is not sent in the clear. It was replaced by RFC 7235, RFC 7615, RFC 7616 and RFC 7617.

eli5.summary: A website asks a visitor for the secret password at the door. In one way you say it plainly; in the other you only show a scrambled proof that you know it.

questions: how does http basic authentication work
what is a nonce in http digest
subtitle: How a web server asks for a password: HTTP's challenge framework, plain Basic, and the hash-based Digest scheme.

tldr.problem: HTTP/1.0 had only Basic authentication, which sends the user name and password over the network as cleartext, and RFC 2069 Digest had problems found after publication.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a generic challenge-response framework (401 with WWW-Authenticate, then an Authorization header), keeps Basic, and specifies Digest, where the client proves it knows the password by sending an MD5 hash that includes a server nonce.
tldr.outcome: Digest avoids sending the password in the clear but gives no confidentiality for the rest of the message. This RFC is obsoleted by RFC 7235, RFC 7615, RFC 7616 and RFC 7617.

today: RFC 2617 is obsoleted by RFC 7235, RFC 7615, RFC 7616 and RFC 7617. It replaced RFC 2069 and is no longer the current definition of HTTP authentication.

sections.title: The Authentication Framework
sections.content:
HTTP offers a simple challenge-response mechanism. A server challenges a request and the client answers with credentials. The scheme is named by a case-insensitive token (auth-scheme), followed by comma-separated name=value parameters.

An origin server challenges with a 401 (Unauthorized) response that MUST carry a WWW-Authenticate header with at least one challenge. A proxy uses 407 (Proxy Authentication Required) with Proxy-Authenticate. The client answers with an Authorization or Proxy-Authorization header. If several challenges are offered, the user agent MUST use the strongest scheme it understands.

Every challenge carries a realm. The realm plus the server's canonical root URL defines the protection space, which lets one server split its resources into areas with separate credentials. Once authorized, the client MAY reuse the same credentials across that space. Proxies MUST forward WWW-Authenticate and Authorization untouched.
sections.eli5: The guard at the door says who is asking and which club room you want. You answer with the right password for that room, and the guard remembers you for the rest of that room.

sections.title: Basic Authentication
sections.content:
In Basic, the client authenticates with a user-ID and password for each realm. The server answers an unauthorized request with a challenge such as WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="WallyWorld". The client replies with the user ID and password joined by a single colon and base64 encoded.

The RFC's example: user ID Aladdin and password open sesame become Authorization: Basic QWxhZGRpbjpvcGVuIHNlc2FtZQ==. There are no optional parameters.

A client SHOULD assume that paths at or below the last path element of the request URI are in the same protection space, and MAY send the header pre-emptively. Base64 is only an encoding, not protection: the abstract says Basic is not considered secure, since the credentials cross the network as cleartext, unless used with something like SSL.
sections.eli5: Basic is like writing your password on a postcard in a code that everybody knows how to undo. Anyone who sees the postcard can read it.

sections.title: How Digest Works
sections.content:
Digest keeps the challenge-response shape but never sends the password. The server's challenge includes a nonce. The client hashes (MD5 by default) its username, the password, the nonce, the HTTP method and the requested URI, and sends the result as response. Both sides must already share the password; how that happens is out of scope.

The challenge may also carry opaque (returned unchanged by the client), domain (URIs in the protection space), stale (true means only the nonce expired, so the client can retry without asking the user again), algorithm (MD5 or MD5-sess) and qop. The qop value auth means authentication, and auth-int adds integrity protection of the body.

When qop is used, the client MUST also send a client nonce cnonce and a request counter nc. The counter is 8 hex digits, so the first request with a nonce sends nc=00000001, and the server can spot replays when it sees the same value twice. The server can send an Authentication-Info header with a nextnonce and a rspauth digest, which lets the client check that the server also knows the secret.

The server does not need the cleartext password, only H(A1), the hash of the username, realm and password. The nonce is up to the server; the RFC suggests a time-stamp plus a hash that includes the ETag and a private key, so the server can limit its lifetime without keeping state.
sections.eli5: The guard gives you a random number. You mix it with your password in a secret blender and hand back the smoothie. The guard has the same blender and checks that the smoothie matches, so the password itself never travels.

sections.title: The Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a request for http://www.nowhere.org/dir/index.html. The user is Mufasa and the password is Circle Of Life. With no Authorization header the server sends 401 Unauthorized with a Digest challenge: realm testrealm@host.com, qop="auth,auth-int", a nonce and an opaque value.

The client prompts the user and retries with username, realm, nonce, uri, qop=auth, nc=00000001, cnonce="0a4f113b", opaque and a 32-hex-digit response, here 6629fae49393a05397450978507c4ef1.

Digest can also authenticate users to proxies, using 407, Proxy-Authenticate and Proxy-Authorization with the same directives. The RFC includes sample C code for the calculations.
sections.eli5: The guard says 'prove it, here is a number'. The visitor comes back with a scrambled answer built from that number, and the guard checks it against his own copy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is frank about the limits. Basic SHOULD NOT be used without enhancements to protect sensitive information, and it is open to counterfeit servers that collect passwords. Digest hides the password, but gives no confidentiality for the rest of the exchange and only limited integrity protection. The RFC says that by modern cryptographic standards Digest is weak, yet far better than Basic.

It lists several attacks and mitigations:

  • Replay: use limited-lifetime or one-time nonces, and auth-int for POST and PUT requests. These choices trade security against performance and request pipelining.
  • Man in the middle: a hostile proxy can offer only Basic. Clients should always use the strongest scheme, show which scheme is in use, or warn before using a weaker one than before.
  • Chosen plaintext, precomputed dictionary and batch brute-force attacks: clients should be configured to require cnonce.
  • Stored passwords: the server's H(A1) file must be protected as if it held cleartext passwords, and the realm string should include the host name.
sections.eli5: Hiding your password is good, but anyone watching can still see everything else you say. Also, a trickster can pretend to be the guard, so always check who you are talking to.
